Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. content.content:
Tutorial: Compose integrations into a system¶ In this tutorial you compose two integrations into a system: a named composition of integrations that are developed and tested independently but run and observed together. You scaffold an extractor that publishes order messages and a loader that consumes them, verify each one alone, then declare their topology in a SystemHost and run the whole flow with one command. The transactional tutorial teaches what happens inside an integration; this one is about what happens between them. Both scaffolds ship with working sample logic, so you won't implement a single pipeline step here — the chapters spend their time on composition. Before you begin¶ You've completed the transactional tutorial — this series assumes its tools and vocabulary and doesn't re-teach pipeline authoring Tools installed: .NET SDK 10, Docker Desktop (running — the system provisions a Redis container), Dapr CLI 1.16+ initialized (dapr init), Task The Intropy CLI installed and on your PATH No separate .NET Aspire install: the SystemHost is an ordinary .NET project, and the orchestration and dashboard arrive as NuGet packages on first restore A scratch directory you don't mind throwing away What you'll build¶ The order-flow system: an order-extractor integration that sweeps order files from an inbound folder and publishes each one as a message, and an order-loader integration that subscribes and writes each order to a destination folder. The message's shape lives in neither of them: the first scaffold also creates a shared Contracts project, and both integrations compile against its Order record. flowchart LR src[(Inbound folder
orders/*.json)]:::ext subgraph sys [system: order-flow] direction LR E[order-extractor
sweep → publish]:::block T{{pub/sub pubsub
topic orders}}:::topic L[order-loader
subscribe → load]:::block E --> T --> L end dst[(Destination folder)]:::ext src --> E L --> dst classDef block fill:#1e1a2e,stroke:#8066FF,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#e6e1f5; classDef topic fill:#0f0d1a,stroke:#8066FF,stroke-width:1px,stroke-dasharray:4 3,color:#e6e1f5; classDef ext fill:#0f0d1a,stroke:#21EAC7,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#cfeee6; style sys fill:#141225,stroke:#8066FF,stroke-width:1px,color:#c8bfe8; The pub/sub in the middle is the interesting part. When an integration runs on its own, that component is private and in-memory: the extractor publishes into a void, and the loader only sees messages you inject by hand. Run through the SystemHost, both sidecars load a system-scoped pub/sub instead — generated from the topology and backed by Redis — and the extractor's messages reach the loader. Same code, same component names, different backing. That resolution rule is the heart of the tutorial. The SystemHost itself is a .NET Aspire AppHost holding the system's source of truth: one class declares the integrations and the typed topic refs that connect them, validated before anything runs. Run it and it starts every integration with its Dapr sidecar, generates and provisions the system-scoped components, and serves a dashboard with logs and traces for the whole system. The same declaration feeds a generation backend, so running locally and generating deployment artifacts are two views of one model. The chapters¶ Each chapter introduces one thing, ends in a runnable command, and leaves you with working code. You can stop after any of them. The extractor — scaffold order-extractor (and the shared Contracts library that comes with it) and run it alone on isolated components The loader — scaffold order-loader against the same shared contract and verify a subscriber in isolation through its own sidecar The SystemHost — scaffold the host and read the typed topology sys create assembled from your scaffolds, then validate it with check System-scoped components — how sidecars resolve components: the local set standalone, the generated overlay under the host Run the system — one command, both integrations, one distributed trace

input.description: Read tutorial chapters 1-2

content.content:
1. The extractor¶
In this chapter you create the system workspace, scaffold the first of its two integrations, and run it alone: a complete integration on its own isolated components, before any system exists.
Scaffold¶
Create the workspace and render the extractor blueprint into it:
mkdir order-flow && cd order-flow
intropy int create extractor -n OrderExtractor -s organization=Fluxia -s topic=orders -o order-extractor

order-flow/ is the system workspace: a plain directory that holds the two integrations and, from chapter 3, the SystemHost as siblings. Nothing about it is special. Each integration stays an independent project you could version, test, and deploy on its own.
Two flags deserve a closer look:

-s topic=orders: the pub/sub topic the extractor publishes to. You'll type the same value when scaffolding the loader — each scaffold declares its own half of the contract, and records it (in .intropy/scaffold.json) for the system to assemble in chapter 3.
No empty=true: unlike the transactional tutorial, you keep the blueprint's sample logic. This tutorial is about what happens between integrations, so the insides stay stock.

The render's last line reports a project you didn't ask for: created dependency Contracts from template shared-contracts. The workspace now holds two directories:
order-flow/
├── Contracts/                    # shared contract types — scaffolded once per workspace
│   ├── Contracts.csproj
│   ├── Order.cs                  # the order contract the extractor publishes
│   └── OrderLine.cs
└── order-extractor/
    ├── Taskfile.yml              # task run / build / test
    ├── docker-compose.yml        # local observability stack — standalone runs only
    ├── local/
    │   ├── dapr-components/
    │   │   ├── poll.yaml         # cron binding — sweeps the inbound folder every 5 s
    │   │   ├── inbound.yaml      # folder binding — stands in for the source system
    │   │   └── pubsub.yaml       # in-memory pub/sub, component name "pubsub"
    │   └── sample-data/
    │       └── sample-order.json
    ├── src/                      # implemented: sweep inbound, transform, publish
    └── test/

The extractor itself looks like the transactional layout you know, with its own components. Contracts/ is new: the extractor template declares the shared-contracts template as a dependency, so scaffolding the first block into a workspace also scaffolds the workspace's contract library next to it. It holds the Order record (and its OrderLine lines): the shape the extractor publishes, defined in neither block because both halves of the system need it. The extractor references it as an ordinary ProjectReference (../../Contracts/Contracts.csproj); its own source shape stays private in src/Model/In.cs, and the pipeline's transform step maps that In to the shared Order before publishing.
The sample logic ships working. On every poll tick it lists the inbound folder, publishes each file's content as an Order message on topic orders, and deletes the source file. And unlike the transactional integration, which runs once and exits, the extractor keeps running until you stop it — that matters in chapter 5, when you'll drop files in while the whole system is live.
Check it¶
Run the extractor standalone:
cd order-extractor
task run

The task seeds sample-order.json into the inbound folder and starts the integration under Dapr, with the sidecar loading only local/dapr-components/. Within a poll tick you should see:
== APP == info: OrderExtractor.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Swept 1 file from inbound
== APP == info: OrderExtractor.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Published ORD-1001 to topic orders (pubsub)

Stop it with Ctrl+C, then confirm the source file is gone:
ls local/storage/inbound/

The folder is empty: the extractor swept the file, published it, and cleaned up.
Where did the message go? Into the extractor's own in-memory pub/sub — and nothing subscribes there. That's the point of an isolated run: it verifies the extractor's whole job (sweep, publish, clean up) without needing a consumer to exist. Delivery to a consumer is the system's job, and that's chapter 5.

Recap

Created the order-flow workspace; integrations and the SystemHost live in it as siblings
Scaffolded order-extractor from the extractor blueprint with its sample logic intact
The render also scaffolded Contracts/, the workspace's shared contract library — the Order record the extractor publishes lives there, not in the extractor
Standalone, the sidecar loads only local/dapr-components/: an isolated, in-memory world
The published message intentionally went nowhere — no consumer exists yet

                
              

                
                  

2. The loader¶
In this chapter you scaffold order-loader, the consuming half of the system, and verify it the way any subscriber is verified in isolation: by publishing through its own sidecar.
Scaffold¶
From the workspace root, render the loader blueprint:
intropy int create loader -n OrderLoader -s organization=Fluxia -s topic=orders -o order-loader

-s topic=orders is the same value you gave the extractor, and typing it twice is deliberate: each integration declares its own half of the contract and stays verifiable alone. Chapter 3 assembles the two halves into one typed declaration — and checks that they meet.
The message shape, though, is not typed twice. The loader template declares the same shared-contracts dependency as the extractor, and this time the render finds the project already in place:
dependency Contracts already scaffolded from shared-contracts — skipped

The first block into a workspace creates Contracts/; every later one detects it by its scaffold record and reuses it. Both blocks now compile against the same Order record, so the shape of the messages crossing the system has exactly one definition.
order-loader/
├── Taskfile.yml
├── docker-compose.yml
├── local/
│   └── dapr-components/
│       ├── pubsub.yaml           # in-memory pub/sub, component name "pubsub"
│       └── destination.yaml      # folder binding — stands in for the destination system
├── src/                          # implemented: subscribe to topic, deserialize, validate, load
└── test/

The sample logic subscribes to orders on pubsub and, for each message, deserializes it into the shared Order record, validates it, and writes {orderId}.json through the destination binding. The mirror image of the extractor's shape handling: the loader consumes the shared Order and maps it to its own private destination shape in src/Model/Out.cs. Like the extractor, it runs until you stop it.
Note that pubsub.yaml here has the same component name as the extractor's — but they are not the same broker. Each in-memory pub/sub lives inside its own integration's sidecar, so two standalone runs are two separate worlds. Keep that in mind; chapter 4 turns it into the mechanism the whole system rests on.
Publish through the loader's own sidecar¶
A subscriber alone has a problem the extractor didn't: nothing publishes to it. The answer follows from where the broker lives. The in-memory pub/sub exists inside the loader's sidecar, so any publish routed through that sidecar reaches the subscription — and dapr publish --publish-app-id does exactly that.
Start the loader in one terminal:
cd order-loader
task run

Wait for the subscription to register:
== APP == info: OrderLoader.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Subscribed to topic orders (pubsub)

Check it¶
In a second terminal, publish an order through the loader's sidecar:
dapr publish --publish-app-id order-loader --pubsub pubsub --topic orders \
  --data '{"orderId":"ORD-2001","customerId":"CUST-42","orderDate":"2026-07-24T09:30:00Z","lines":[{"sku":"SKU-AAA","quantity":1,"unitPrice":12.50}]}'

Event published successfully

The loader picks it up and writes the destination file:
cat local/storage/destination/ORD-2001.json

{"OrderId":"ORD-2001","CustomerId":"CUST-42","LoadedAt":"2026-07-24T09:31:12Z","Status":"Loaded"}

Stop the loader with Ctrl+C.

Recap

Scaffolded order-loader: subscribes to orders on pubsub, writes each order through the destination binding
The loader's render found Contracts/ already scaffolded and skipped it — both blocks compile against one shared Order record
A subscriber is verified in isolation by publishing through its own sidecar — that's where its in-memory broker lives
Both integrations now work alone, each in its own isolated world; nothing connects them yet

The public API surface of src/Intropy.Topology: SystemBuilder methods (list ALL builder methods with signatures, e.g. AddIntegration, AddTopic, AddApi, AddConnector, etc.), the Refs types (Refs.cs), Components.cs, Discovery.cs, and the Model/ types (SystemTopology, Edges, ComponentModel, Resources, Enums — list the record/class definitions and their properties).

7. The examples/OrderFulfillment.SystemHost — what does its system declaration use (which builder calls appear in OrderFulfillmentSystem.cs, Topics.cs, Apis.cs, Connectors.cs)?

content.text:
# Intropy.Topology — complete feature inventory (branch `feature/file-transport`)

Repo root: `/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/Intropy.Topology`
Solution file: `/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/Intropy.Topology/Intropy.Topology.slnx` (13 projects). No `.sln`; central package management via `Directory.Packages.props`, shared props in `Directory.Build.props` (net10.0, nullable, `TreatWarningsAsErrors`, `AnalysisMode=All`).

**Important correction to your premise:** there is **no** `AddIntegration`, `AddTopic`, `AddApi`, or `AddConnector`. `SystemBuilder` has exactly four `Add*` methods (block kinds). Topics/APIs/connectors are declared as **static fields** via `TopicRef<T>.Define` / `ApiRef<T>.Define` / `ConnectorRef.Define` and the resources **materialize from usage**. Also: no state store, no bindings-as-builder, no `Uses`/platform services, no ContainerService, no Reconciler — CLAUDE.md says those were deliberately cut ("this is a lean PoC").

---

## 1. Projects in the solution

### src (3, all packable NuGet libs)
| Project | Purpose |

- `DuplicatePortRule` (:10) — **ITP101** error: output port names unique per component (two bare `Publishes(topic)` collide on `default`), and one topic not published via two ports of the same component.
- `DuplicateSubscriptionRule` (:49) — **ITP102** error: no component subscribes to the same topic twice.
- `TopicContractConflictRule` (:72) — **ITP103** error: one topic must not be used with two different contract types.

## 5. `src/Intropy.Topology.Aspire` (554 LOC)

**`IntropyAspire.cs`** (360 lines) — `public static class IntropyAspire` (:19), the only public type in the package:
- `public static Task<int> RunAsync(Assembly, string[] args)` (:31) — discovers system, builds `DevManifest`, generates Dev artifacts into `%TEMP%/intropy-aspire/<system>-<guid>`, applies to a `DistributedApplication`, runs it.
- `internal static void Apply(IDistributedApplicationBuilder, SystemTopology, DevManifest, string generatedRoot)` (:55) — the meat, separated for testability. What it does:
  - Fails fast on any connector with no transport (:60-70).
  - Adds a raw Redis 8 container on fixed port 6379 (`RedisPort` const :23) — deliberately not `AddRedis` (TLS mismatch with generated plaintext YAML).
  - Adds one container per `DevMock` external system with optional fixed/target ports.
  - Adds **one Microcks instance** (`AddMicrocks`, pinned to `DevHttpMock.Port` 8585) loading all `HttpApiMocks` + `ApiMocks` OpenAPI artifacts (:106-119).
  - Registers `BeforeResourceStartedEvent` hook (:127) that gates every `*-dapr-cli` sidecar on TCP readiness of all backends and, for publishers, on subscriber sidecars reaching Running.
  - Per component: stages a component overlay, then either `AddContainer` (if a `DevBuilder.Override` image exists) or `AddProject` resolved by folder convention + `WithHttpEndpoint()`; throws listing unresolved components (:189).
  - Skips components whose every provided API is dev-mocked (`MockedApiProviders`, :290) — with validation that a provider can only be skipped whole.
  - Derives **subscriber-first startup ordering** from topics (`SubscriberPrecedence` :234) with cycle detection (`HasCycle` :261) that degrades to a stderr warning.
  - `Wire<T>` (:331) attaches the Dapr sidecar (`WithDaprSidecar`, AppId = component name, `ResourcesPaths = [staged]`) and injects `INTROPY__COMPONENT` and `INTROPY__CONFIG` env vars.

**`ComponentOverlay.cs`** (90 lines, internal) — `Stage(appHostDirectory, componentName, generatedComponentsDir)` (:15): copies the integration's own `local/dapr-components/*.yaml` then overlays the system's generated components, replacing by top-level `metadata.name` and adding new ones, into `<appHost>/obj/dapr-components/<component>/`. `MetadataName(yaml)` (:60) is a hand-rolled YAML sniffer that only accepts the unindented `metadata:` block (avoids `spec.metadata`).

**`ProjectConvention.cs`** (33 lines, internal) — `IntegrationRoot` (:13) = `../<component>/` sibling of the AppHost; `Resolve` (:17) = single `src/*.csproj` inside it, else flat `<name>.csproj`; `LocalComponentsDir` (:31) = `<root>/local/dapr-components`.

**`TcpReadyHealthCheck.cs`** (68 lines, internal `IHealthCheck`) — connects and requires the connection to survive a 750 ms read window (Docker Desktop's port proxy accepts before the process listens). `WaitUntilReadyAsync(timeout, ct)` (:17) polls at 1 s.

## Notes for "minimal core" planning

Natural seams, cheapest-to-cut first:

1. **`Intropy.Topology.Aspire` (554 LOC + 4 packages)** is the only dependency-bearing project and depends on Docker, the Dapr CLI, and Microcks at runtime. Dropping it makes the whole product dependency-free.
2. **Dev mocking (`DevProfile.cs`, 256 of Generation's 732 LOC)** is a self-contained seam — `IDevProfile`/`DevBuilder`/`DevManifest`/3 mock records — used only by the Aspire backend and the Dev generation profile. Cut it and `Generate(topology, profile)` collapses to ~150 LOC.
3. **The unresolved-connector feature** cuts across 4 `ConnectorRef.Define` overloads, nullable `System`/`Transport`, materializer facet-upgrading, ITP104's null-skipping, ITP107, the generator's TODO-comment path, and Aspire's fail-fast. Keeping only the fully-resolved `Define(name, system, transport)` removes ~120 LOC spread across 5 files.
4. **Transports** — 5 concrete types + JSON polymorphism; a minimal core could keep only `Transport.Custom(daprType, in, out)` or two concrete ones, dropping ITP105/ITP106 too.
5. **Truly irreducible core** ≈ `SystemBuilder` + `ComponentBuilders` + `Components` + `Model/` + `TopologyMaterializer` + `NameRules` + a handful of rules ≈ **900–1,000 LOC**, zero dependencies.
6. Every current feature has test coverage at roughly 1:1 LOC with src (1,913 test LOC against 1,918 core LOC), so cuts will remove comparable test volume — `Validation/RuleTests.cs` alone is 651 lines.

## Notes for "minimal core" planning

Natural seams, cheapest-to-cut first:

1. **`Intropy.Topology.Aspire` (554 LOC + 4 packages)** is the only dependency-bearing project and depends on Docker, the Dapr CLI, and Microcks at runtime. Dropping it makes the whole product dependency-free.
2. **Dev mocking (`DevProfile.cs`, 256 of Generation's 732 LOC)** is a self-contained seam — `IDevProfile`/`DevBuilder`/`DevManifest`/3 mock records — used only by the Aspire backend and the Dev generation profile. Cut it and `Generate(topology, profile)` collapses to ~150 LOC.
3. **The unresolved-connector feature** cuts across 4 `ConnectorRef.Define` overloads, nullable `System`/`Transport`, materializer facet-upgrading, ITP104's null-skipping, ITP107, the generator's TODO-comment path, and Aspire's fail-fast. Keeping only the fully-resolved `Define(name, system, transport)` removes ~120 LOC spread across 5 files.
4. **Transports** — 5 concrete types + JSON polymorphism; a minimal core could keep only `Transport.Custom(daprType, in, out)` or two concrete ones, dropping ITP105/ITP106 too.
5. **Truly irreducible core** ≈ `SystemBuilder` + `ComponentBuilders` + `Components` + `Model/` + `TopologyMaterializer` + `NameRules` + a handful of rules ≈ **900–1,000 LOC**, zero dependencies.
6. Every current feature has test coverage at roughly 1:1 LOC with src (1,913 test LOC against 1,918 core LOC), so cuts will remove comparable test volume — `Validation/RuleTests.cs` alone is 651 lines.

content.content:
3. The SystemHost¶
In this chapter you scaffold the SystemHost and read the file it exists for: the system's topology,
declared as typed C# and validated before anything runs.
A SystemHost is a .NET Aspire AppHost with one Intropy-specific job: it holds the system's source
of truth. One class declares which integrations exist and which topics connect them; everything
else the host does — running the system locally, generating its Dapr components, validating the
composition — is a backend over that one declaration. There is nothing to install; the
orchestration, the dashboard, and the topology model arrive as NuGet packages on first restore.
Scaffold¶
From the workspace root:

content.content:
4. System-scoped components¶
In this chapter you learn how the same integration code loads different Dapr components depending on who starts it: its own local set when run standalone, the system's generated overlay under the SystemHost.
One file you wrote, one the host generates¶
Open the extractor's pub/sub component:
order-extractor/local/dapr-components/pubsub.yamlapiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: pubsub
spec:
  type: pubsub.in-memory
  version: v1

The system's counterpart is not a file you wrote. There is no dapr-components/ directory in system-host/, and chapter 3's declaration never mentioned Redis. The host derives it: Topics.Orders names a pubsub component called pubsub, so the run backend generates one, backed by Redis because that is what the local run profile provisions:
system-host/obj/dapr-components/order-extractor/pubsub.yaml (generated)apiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: pubsub
spec:
  type: pubsub.redis
  version: v1
  metadata:
    - name: redisHost
      value: localhost:6379

Same metadata.name, different spec.type. That shared name is the whole mechanism: application code addresses components by name and never learns which backing is behind it. Whoever starts the sidecar decides which file the name resolves to — and on the system side that file is generated from the topology, so the model you validated in chapter 3 and the YAML the sidecar loads cannot disagree.
The overlay¶
Standalone, you've already seen the answer: task run starts the sidecar with --resources-path ./local/dapr-components, so the integration gets its isolated, in-memory world.
Under the SystemHost, the host stages an effective component set for each integration before starting its sidecar:

Generate the system's components from the topology: one Redis-backed pubsub, because Topics.Orders names it.
Copy everything from the integration's local/dapr-components/.
Overlay the generated components: a generated component with the same metadata.name replaces the local one; new names are added.
Start the sidecar with --resources-path pointing at the staged directory, under system-host/obj/dapr-components/<integration-name>/.

For the extractor that means poll.yaml and inbound.yaml pass through untouched — sweeping a local folder is the integration's own business in both modes — while the local pubsub.yaml is replaced by the generated one.
Why an overlay, rather than handing the sidecar both directories? Because Dapr refuses duplicate component names across resource paths, and the duplicate name is the mechanism. And why not have the host generate a complete set? Then the topology would have to describe every folder binding in every integration — concerns that are the integration's own business, not the system's.
The overlay has edges worth knowing: it is staged when the host starts, so changing the topology means restarting the SystemHost; it keys on metadata.name, not the filename; and a generated component applies to every integration in the system. The Redis port is pinned to 6379, so the YAML above is exactly what the sidecars load. The staged files are real YAML on disk — inspect them whenever resolution surprises you — but editing them is futile: they are regenerated from the model on every start. Change the declaration, not the artifacts.
Check it¶
Start the system for the first time:
cd system-host
dotnet run

Leave it running and, from the workspace root in a second terminal, inspect what was staged for the extractor:
ls system-host/obj/dapr-components/order-extractor/

inbound.yaml  poll.yaml  pubsub.yaml

grep "type:" system-host/obj/dapr-components/order-extractor/pubsub.yaml

  type: pubsub.redis

The two local components passed through; the pub/sub is now the system's — generated, not written. Stop the host with Ctrl+C — the next chapter runs it for real.

Recap

Component resolution is decided by whoever starts the sidecar: the local directory standalone, the staged overlay under the SystemHost
Local components pass through untouched; a generated component with the same metadata.name replaces its local counterpart
The system's components are generated from chapter 3's declaration; the staged set under obj/ is inspectable, but regenerated on every start
Code and component names are identical in both modes; only the backing changes

                
              

                
                  

5. Run the system¶
In this chapter you run the whole system with one command and follow a single order from the extractor's inbound folder, across the system-scoped pub/sub, to the loader's destination: one message, one distributed trace.
Start it¶
cd system-host
dotnet run

info: Aspire.Hosting.DistributedApplication[0]
      Distributed application starting.
info: Aspire.Hosting.DistributedApplication[0]
      Login to the dashboard at https://localhost:17178/login?t=<token>

Open the dashboard URL. The resources page shows the whole system: order-extractor and order-loader with their Dapr sidecars, and redis — the container the host provisioned because chapter 3's declaration names a pubsub — all Running. Watch the startup order: the loader came up and registered its subscription before the extractor began polling. Nobody declared that; the host derived it from the topology — Topics.Orders says who subscribes and who publishes, and subscribers start first.
One thing is conspicuously absent: the Grafana stack from the standalone runs. The SystemHost injects OTLP endpoints into every integration it starts, so logs, metrics, and traces from the whole system land in the Aspire dashboard instead.
Send an order through¶
With the system running, drop the sample order into the extractor's inbound folder:
cp order-extractor/local/sample-data/sample-order.json order-extractor/local/storage/inbound/

Within a poll tick the extractor sweeps it and publishes — and this time the message doesn't vanish into an in-memory void. It crosses the system-scoped Redis pub/sub and lands in the loader's subscription.
Check it¶
cat order-loader/local/storage/destination/ORD-1001.json

{"OrderId":"ORD-1001","CustomerId":"CUST-42","LoadedAt":"2026-07-24T10:02:41Z","Status":"Loaded"}

The order made the full crossing. Now open the dashboard's Traces page and select the newest trace: one trace, spans from both integrations:
order-extractor   publish orders (pubsub)        12 ms
└─ order-loader   process orders (pubsub)         8 ms
   └─ order-loader   load ORD-1001                3 ms

The trace context rode the pub/sub hop inside the message's CloudEvents envelope, which is why two separate processes show up as one story. In chapters 1 and 2 these were two isolated worlds; the only thing that changed is who started the sidecars.

Recap
You composed a system:

Two integrations, each scaffolded, run, and verified alone on isolated in-memory components
A SystemHost holding the topology as a typed declaration: two integrations sharing one TopicRef, validated before anything started
Under the host, sidecars load the system-scoped overlay: pubsub backed by Redis, folder bindings untouched
Neither integration changed by a single line between chapter 2 and now
The whole flow is observable as one distributed trace across both integrations

That last invariant is the discipline to keep: an integration earns its place in a system by working alone first.

Two integrations, each scaffolded, run, and verified alone on isolated in-memory components

# Minimal Intropy.Topology supporting the system tutorial

## Context

`tooling/Intropy.Topology` (branch `feature/file-transport`, clean tree, HEAD `09ce919` = main + file-transport commit) has grown to ~3,200 src LOC across three NuGet packages, much of it for features the current product surface doesn't use. The authoritative spec for what must keep working is the system tutorial (http://127.0.0.1:8000/tutorials/system/) **plus** what `intropy sys create` actually generates (`intropy-cli/internal/system/codegen.go` emits `From`/`To` edges with `ConnectorRef.Define(name, Transport.File("./test/<name>"))` — the tutorial page omits connectors, but the CLI is the real consumer).

Decisions confirmed with the user:
- **Keep file connectors** (transport-only `ConnectorRef.Define` + `Transport.File`); cut all other transports and the unresolved-connector machinery. No intropy-cli changes needed.
- **Replace examples** with a tutorial-shaped order-flow system.
- **Branching:** preserve everything on a `full-topology` branch; land the minimal version on `main`.

Expected outcome: src shrinks from ~3,200 to roughly 1,600–1,800 LOC, `Intropy.Topology` and `.Generation` stay dependency-free, `.Aspire` drops the Microcks dependency.

## Repo & branching

All work in `/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/Intropy.Topology`.
(Note: `~/dev/intropy/intropy-topology` is a separate, older single-commit repo with a different model shape — not touched.)

1. `git branch full-topology 09ce919` — preserves the current full version for later reapplication.
2. Work on `feature/minimal-core` branched from `09ce919` (minimal needs the `Transport.File` commit).
3. Land on `main` when done (merge/PR). No remote is configured locally; if one exists elsewhere, push `full-topology` too.

## What the tutorial + CLI actually require (keep list)

- `SystemBuilder`: `Create`, `AddExtractor`, `AddLoader`, `Build`, `TryBuild`, `Validate` (`src/Intropy.Topology/SystemBuilder.cs`)
- `ExtractorBuilder`: `From(ConnectorRef)`, `Publishes(TopicRef)`; `LoaderBuilder`: `Subscribes(TopicRef)`, `To(ConnectorRef)` (`Building/ComponentBuilders.cs`)
- `TopicRef<T>.Define(pubsub, topic)`; `ConnectorRef.Define(name, Transport)`; `Transport.File(rootPath)` (`Refs.cs`)
- `ISystemDefinition` + `SystemDiscovery` (`Discovery.cs`)
- Validation incl. ITP208/ITP209 (demonstrated in tutorial ch. 3)
- `IntropyGenerate.RunAsync` with `check`, `graph`, `generate` verbs (`generate` referenced by the system-host template's Taskfile)
- `IntropyAspire.RunAsync`: Redis container, component overlay, subscriber-first ordering, Dapr sidecars with `INTROPY__COMPONENT`/`INTROPY__CONFIG`, project-by-convention resolution, TCP readiness gating

## Changes by project

### 1. `src/Intropy.Topology` (core)

**Delete outright:**
- `AddAggregator`/`AddTransactionalIntegration` + `AggregatorBuilder`/`TransactionalIntegrationBuilder` + `AggregatorComponent`/`TransactionalIntegrationComponent`
- Entire API feature: `ApiRef`/`ApiRef<T>`, `Provides`/`Consumes` (incl. base-builder `Consumes`), `ApiResource`, provide/consume call tracking in `Components.cs`, `Validation/Rules/ApiRules.cs` (ITP501)
- Named publish ports: remove `Publishes(string port, TopicRef)` overload (keep the internal `Port = "default"` field on `PublishEdge` so the generated config JSON schema doesn't churn — the framework's config binding is still landing)
- Transports `Http`/`Sftp`/`Blob`/`Custom` and their record types; keep `Transport` (abstract, for the JSON-polymorphic seam) + `FileTransport` only
- Unresolved-connector machinery: the 1-arg/`ExternalSystem` `ConnectorRef.Define` overloads, `ExternalSystem` record, nullable `System`/`Transport`, materializer facet-upgrading (`Building/TopologyMaterializer.cs:165`), ITP107 (`UnresolvedConnectorRule`), ITP105/ITP106 (`ConnectorCapabilityRules.cs` — FileTransport supports both directions, nothing left to check)

**Keep (simplify where noted):**
- `Model/`: `SystemTopology` (drop `Apis`), `ComponentModel` (drop `Provides`/`Consumes`), `Edges.cs` as-is, `TopicResource`, `ConnectorResource` (drop `ExternalSystemName`, make `Transport` non-nullable), `ComponentKind` → `{Extractor, Loader}`, `ConnectorDirection`
- `TopologyMaterializer` (drop API accumulator + facet upgrading)
- `Discovery.cs`, `TopologyDiagnostic`, `TopologyValidationException`, `NameRules` unchanged
- Rules kept: ITP001, ITP002 (`StructureRules.cs`), ITP101 (simplified — only duplicate-publish on default port), ITP102, ITP103, ITP104 (simplified — transport equality only) (`TopicAndConnectorRules.cs`), ITP206, ITP207, ITP208, ITP209 (`CompletenessRules.cs`), ITP302, ITP401 (`UsageAndCollisionRules.cs`)
- Update the retired-codes comment in `Validation/TopologyRules.cs:8-13` to also record ITP105/106/107/501 as retired-in-minimal

### 2. `src/Intropy.Topology.Generation`

- **Delete `DevProfile.cs` entirely** (`IDevProfile`, `DevBuilder`, `DevManifest`, `DevHttpMock`, `DevApiMock`, `DevMock` — 256 LOC)
- `Generation.cs`: drop `GenerationProfile` enum and the Prod branch — `TopologyGenerator.Generate(topology)` always emits the local/dev artifacts: `components/<pubsub>.yaml` (pubsub.redis, scoped), `components/binding.<connector>.yaml` (bindings.localstorage + absolutized `rootPath`), `config/<component>.intropy.json`. Drop `HttpEndpointForMockedApi`, mock-URL metadata resolution, and the unresolved-transport TODO path. Keep the hand-rolled `DaprYaml` emitter.
- `IntropyGenerate.cs`: keep `check`/`graph`/`generate` verbs; drop `--profile` parsing; `graph` projection drops apis/provides/consumes and the `"(unresolved)"` transport display.

### 3. `src/Intropy.Topology.Aspire`

- `IntropyAspire.cs`: keep `RunAsync` + `Apply` (signature loses the `DevManifest` parameter). Drop: Microcks (`AddMicrocks`, mock artifact loading), `DevMock` external-system containers, component image overrides (the `AddContainer` path), `MockedApiProviders` skipping, and the unresolved-transport fail-fast (transport is now always resolved). Keep: Redis 8 container on 6379, `BeforeResourceStartedEvent` readiness gating, subscriber-first ordering with cycle detection, `Wire` (sidecar, resources path, env vars).
- Keep `ComponentOverlay.cs`, `ProjectConvention.cs`, `TcpReadyHealthCheck.cs` unchanged.
- csproj: drop `Microcks.Aspire`; keep `Aspire.Hosting`, `Aspire.Hosting.Redis`, `CommunityToolkit.Aspire.Hosting.Dapr`. Remove the Microcks entry from `Directory.Packages.props`.

### 4. `examples/`

Replace `OrderFulfillment.*` + the five worker stubs with a tutorial-shaped system (reuse the existing 14-line worker-stub pattern):
- `examples/OrderFlow.Contracts` — `Order`/`OrderLine` records
- `examples/order-extractor`, `examples/order-loader` — worker stubs (env-var echo + `MapGet`), each with `local/dapr-components/` matching the tutorial (in-memory `pubsub.yaml` etc.) so the overlay is exercised
- `examples/OrderFlow.SystemHost` — `Program.cs` (two-backend dispatch, verbatim from the CLI's system-host skeleton), `Topics.cs`, `Connectors.cs`, `OrderFlowSystem.cs` **matching `sys create` codegen output exactly** (golden output in `intropy-cli/internal/system/create_test.go:173-210`) — this doubles as a compile-time guarantee that CLI-generated code builds against the minimal library
- Delete stale `examples/graph.json` and `examples/workloads/`
- Update `Intropy.Topology.slnx` project list accordingly

### 5. Tests

Prune to the surviving surface (test LOC tracks src ~1:1):
- `test/Intropy.Topology.Test`: drop aggregator/transactional/API/port/transport/unresolved cases from `RefTests`, `ComponentTests`, `Building/*`, `Validation/RuleTests.cs` (651 lines — largest cut); keep/adapt everything covering the keep-list, especially ITP208/209 and connector-with-file-transport materialization
- `test/Intropy.Topology.Generation.Test`: drop `DevProfileTests.cs`, Prod-profile and httpendpoint cases; retarget `TestSystem.cs` to extractor+loader+file connectors
- `test/Intropy.Topology.Aspire.Test`: drop Microcks/mock/override cases and `mocks/*.yaml`; keep overlay + ordering + wiring tests

### 6. Docs in repo

- Rewrite `CLAUDE.md` and `README.md` for the reduced surface
- `docs/concepts/`: delete `apis.md`; trim `connectors.md` (file transport only), `validation.md` (rule table), `topics.md`/`materialization.md` (remove port/API mentions)
- Leave `docs/decisions/` ADRs untouched (historical record); optionally add a short ADR 0009 "minimal core for the system tutorial; full model preserved on `full-topology`"

## Out of scope (flag, don't do)

- intropy-cli and intropy-templates need **no changes** (connectors kept). The template pins `Intropy.Topology.* 0.2.0`; releasing the minimal as `v0.3.0` (tag-driven `release.yml`) and bumping the template pin is a follow-up.
- The tutorial docs page showing no `Connectors.cs`/`From`/`To` is stale relative to the CLI — flag to fix in intropy-techdocs separately.
- Reapplying full features later = merge/cherry-pick from `full-topology`.

## Verification

1. `dotnet build` + `dotnet test` at repo root (all three test projects green).
2. From `examples/OrderFlow.SystemHost`: `dotnet run -- check` → `ok: 'order-flow' is valid (2 components)`; `dotnet run -- graph` → matches tutorial ch. 3 JSON shape (+ connectors); `dotnet run -- generate ./out` → pubsub yaml + 2 binding yamls + 2 config JSONs.
3. Live run (Docker + Dapr required): `dotnet run` from the example host — dashboard up, Redis provisioned, both sidecars start subscriber-first; verify `obj/dapr-components/order-extractor/pubsub.yaml` shows `pubsub.redis` (tutorial ch. 4 check).
4. End-to-end tutorial flow if desired: scaffold ch. 1–3 with the intropy CLI in a scratch dir, point the SystemHost csproj at the local minimal packages (`dotnet pack` + local feed), run `check`/`graph`/`run`.
5. Suggest commit points per phase (branch setup / core cut / generation / aspire / examples+tests / docs) — no auto-commits.

## Context

`tooling/Intropy.Topology` (branch `feature/file-transport`, clean tree, HEAD `09ce919` = main + file-transport commit) has grown to ~3,200 src LOC across three NuGet packages, much of it for features the current product surface doesn't use. The authoritative spec for what must keep working is the system tutorial (http://127.0.0.1:8000/tutorials/system/) **plus** what `intropy sys create` actually generates (`intropy-cli/internal/system/codegen.go` emits `From`/`To` edges with `ConnectorRef.Define(name, Transport.File("./test/<name>"))` — the tutorial page omits connectors, but the CLI is the real consumer).

Decisions confirmed with the user:
- **Keep file connectors** (transport-only `ConnectorRef.Define` + `Transport.File`); cut all other transports and the unresolved-connector machinery. No intropy-cli changes needed.
- **Replace examples** with a tutorial-shaped order-flow system.
- **Branching:** preserve everything on a `full-topology` branch; land the minimal version on `main`.

Expected outcome: src shrinks from ~3,200 to roughly 1,600–1,800 LOC, `Intropy.Topology` and `.Generation` stay dependency-free, `.Aspire` drops the Microcks dependency.

## Repo & branching

All work in `/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/Intropy.Topology`.
(Note: `~/dev/intropy/intropy-topology` is a separate, older single-commit repo with a different model shape — not touched.)

1. `git branch full-topology 09ce919` — preserves the current full version for later reapplication.
2. Work on `feature/minimal-core` branched from `09ce919` (minimal needs the `Transport.File` commit).
3. Land on `main` when done (merge/PR). No remote is configured locally; if one exists elsewhere, push `full-topology` too.

## What the tutorial + CLI actually require (keep list)

- `SystemBuilder`: `Create`, `AddExtractor`, `AddLoader`, `Build`, `TryBuild`, `Validate` (`src/Intropy.Topology/SystemBuilder.cs`)
- `ExtractorBuilder`: `From(ConnectorRef)`, `Publishes(TopicRef)`; `LoaderBuilder`: `Subscribes(TopicRef)`, `To(ConnectorRef)` (`Building/ComponentBuilders.cs`)
- `TopicRef<T>.Define(pubsub, topic)`; `ConnectorRef.Define(name, Transport)`; `Transport.File(rootPath)` (`Refs.cs`)
- `ISystemDefinition` + `SystemDiscovery` (`Discovery.cs`)
- Validation incl. ITP208/ITP209 (demonstrated in tutorial ch. 3)
- `IntropyGenerate.RunAsync` with `check`, `graph`, `generate` verbs (`generate` referenced by the system-host template's Taskfile)
- `IntropyAspire.RunAsync`: Redis container, component overlay, subscriber-first ordering, Dapr sidecars with `INTROPY__COMPONENT`/`INTROPY__CONFIG`, project-by-convention resolution, TCP readiness gating

## Changes by project

### 1. `src/Intropy.Topology` (core)

**Delete outright:**
- `AddAggregator`/`AddTransactionalIntegration` + `AggregatorBuilder`/`TransactionalIntegrationBuilder` + `AggregatorComponent`/`TransactionalIntegrationComponent`
- Entire API feature: `ApiRef`/`ApiRef<T>`, `Provides`/`Consumes` (incl. base-builder `Consumes`), `ApiResource`, provide/consume call tracking in `Components.cs`, `Validation/Rules/ApiRules.cs` (ITP501)
- Named publish ports: remove `Publishes(string port, TopicRef)` overload (keep the internal `Port = "default"` field on `PublishEdge` so the generated config JSON schema doesn't churn — the framework's config binding is still landing)
- Transports `Http`/`Sftp`/`Blob`/`Custom` and their record types; keep `Transport` (abstract, for the JSON-polymorphic seam) + `FileTransport` only
- Unresolved-connector machinery: the 1-arg/`ExternalSystem` `ConnectorRef.Define` overloads, `ExternalSystem` record, nullable `System`/`Transport`, materializer facet-upgrading (`Building/TopologyMaterializer.cs:165`), ITP107 (`UnresolvedConnectorRule`), ITP105/ITP106 (`ConnectorCapabilityRules.cs` — FileTransport supports both directions, nothing left to check)

**Keep (simplify where noted):**
- `Model/`: `SystemTopology` (drop `Apis`), `ComponentModel` (drop `Provides`/`Consumes`), `Edges.cs` as-is, `TopicResource`, `ConnectorResource` (drop `ExternalSystemName`, make `Transport` non-nullable), `ComponentKind` → `{Extractor, Loader}`, `ConnectorDirection`
- `TopologyMaterializer` (drop API accumulator + facet upgrading)
- `Discovery.cs`, `TopologyDiagnostic`, `TopologyValidationException`, `NameRules` unchanged
- Rules kept: ITP001, ITP002 (`StructureRules.cs`), ITP101 (simplified — only duplicate-publish on default port), ITP102, ITP103, ITP104 (simplified — transport equality only) (`TopicAndConnectorRules.cs`), ITP206, ITP207, ITP208, ITP209 (`CompletenessRules.cs`), ITP302, ITP401 (`UsageAndCollisionRules.cs`)
- Update the retired-codes comment in `Validation/TopologyRules.cs:8-13` to also record ITP105/106/107/501 as retired-in-minimal

### 2. `src/Intropy.Topology.Generation`

- **Delete `DevProfile.cs` entirely** (`IDevProfile`, `DevBuilder`, `DevManifest`, `DevHttpMock`, `DevApiMock`, `DevMock` — 256 LOC)
- `Generation.cs`: drop `GenerationProfile` enum and the Prod branch — `TopologyGenerator.Generate(topology)` always emits the local/dev artifacts: `components/<pubsub>.yaml` (pubsub.redis, scoped), `components/binding.<connector>.yaml` (bindings.localstorage + absolutized `rootPath`), `config/<component>.intropy.json`. Drop `HttpEndpointForMockedApi`, mock-URL metadata resolution, and the unresolved-transport TODO path. Keep the hand-rolled `DaprYaml` emitter.
- `IntropyGenerate.cs`: keep `check`/`graph`/`generate` verbs; drop `--profile` parsing; `graph` projection drops apis/provides/consumes and the `"(unresolved)"` transport display.

### 3. `src/Intropy.Topology.Aspire`

- `IntropyAspire.cs`: keep `RunAsync` + `Apply` (signature loses the `DevManifest` parameter). Drop: Microcks (`AddMicrocks`, mock artifact loading), `DevMock` external-system containers, component image overrides (the `AddContainer` path), `MockedApiProviders` skipping, and the unresolved-transport fail-fast (transport is now always resolved). Keep: Redis 8 container on 6379, `BeforeResourceStartedEvent` readiness gating, subscriber-first ordering with cycle detection, `Wire` (sidecar, resources path, env vars).
- Keep `ComponentOverlay.cs`, `ProjectConvention.cs`, `TcpReadyHealthCheck.cs` unchanged.
- csproj: drop `Microcks.Aspire`; keep `Aspire.Hosting`, `Aspire.Hosting.Redis`, `CommunityToolkit.Aspire.Hosting.Dapr`. Remove the Microcks entry from `Directory.Packages.props`.

### 4. `examples/`

Replace `OrderFulfillment.*` + the five worker stubs with a tutorial-shaped system (reuse the existing 14-line worker-stub pattern):
- `examples/OrderFlow.Contracts` — `Order`/`OrderLine` records
- `examples/order-extractor`, `examples/order-loader` — worker stubs (env-var echo + `MapGet`), each with `local/dapr-components/` matching the tutorial (in-memory `pubsub.yaml` etc.) so the overlay is exercised
- `examples/OrderFlow.SystemHost` — `Program.cs` (two-backend dispatch, verbatim from the CLI's system-host skeleton), `Topics.cs`, `Connectors.cs`, `OrderFlowSystem.cs` **matching `sys create` codegen output exactly** (golden output in `intropy-cli/internal/system/create_test.go:173-210`) — this doubles as a compile-time guarantee that CLI-generated code builds against the minimal library
- Delete stale `examples/graph.json` and `examples/workloads/`
- Update `Intropy.Topology.slnx` project list accordingly

### 5. Tests

Prune to the surviving surface (test LOC tracks src ~1:1):
- `test/Intropy.Topology.Test`: drop aggregator/transactional/API/port/transport/unresolved cases from `RefTests`, `ComponentTests`, `Building/*`, `Validation/RuleTests.cs` (651 lines — largest cut); keep/adapt everything covering the keep-list, especially ITP208/209 and connector-with-file-transport materialization
- `test/Intropy.Topology.Generation.Test`: drop `DevProfileTests.cs`, Prod-profile and httpendpoint cases; retarget `TestSystem.cs` to extractor+loader+file connectors
- `test/Intropy.Topology.Aspire.Test`: drop Microcks/mock/override cases and `mocks/*.yaml`; keep overlay + ordering + wiring tests

### 6. Docs in repo

- Rewrite `CLAUDE.md` and `README.md` for the reduced surface
- `docs/concepts/`: delete `apis.md`; trim `connectors.md` (file transport only), `validation.md` (rule table), `topics.md`/`materialization.md` (remove port/API mentions)
- Leave `docs/decisions/` ADRs untouched (historical record); optionally add a short ADR 0009 "minimal core for the system tutorial; full model preserved on `full-topology`"

## Out of scope (flag, don't do)

- intropy-cli and intropy-templates need **no changes** (connectors kept). The template pins `Intropy.Topology.* 0.2.0`; releasing the minimal as `v0.3.0` (tag-driven `release.yml`) and bumping the template pin is a follow-up.
- The tutorial docs page showing no `Connectors.cs`/`From`/`To` is stale relative to the CLI — flag to fix in intropy-techdocs separately.
- Reapplying full features later = merge/cherry-pick from `full-topology`.

## Verification

1. `dotnet build` + `dotnet test` at repo root (all three test projects green).
2. From `examples/OrderFlow.SystemHost`: `dotnet run -- check` → `ok: 'order-flow' is valid (2 components)`; `dotnet run -- graph` → matches tutorial ch. 3 JSON shape (+ connectors); `dotnet run -- generate ./out` → pubsub yaml + 2 binding yamls + 2 config JSONs.
3. Live run (Docker + Dapr required): `dotnet run` from the example host — dashboard up, Redis provisioned, both sidecars start subscriber-first; verify `obj/dapr-components/order-extractor/pubsub.yaml` shows `pubsub.redis` (tutorial ch. 4 check).
4. End-to-end tutorial flow if desired: scaffold ch. 1–3 with the intropy CLI in a scratch dir, point the SystemHost csproj at the local minimal packages (`dotnet pack` + local feed), run `check`/`graph`/`run`.
5. Suggest commit points per phase (branch setup / core cut / generation / aspire / examples+tests / docs) — no auto-commits.

# Minimal Intropy.Topology supporting the system tutorial

## Context

`tooling/Intropy.Topology` (branch `feature/file-transport`, clean tree, HEAD `09ce919` = main + file-transport commit) has grown to ~3,200 src LOC across three NuGet packages, much of it for features the current product surface doesn't use. The authoritative spec for what must keep working is the system tutorial (http://127.0.0.1:8000/tutorials/system/) **plus** what `intropy sys create` actually generates (`intropy-cli/internal/system/codegen.go` emits `From`/`To` edges with `ConnectorRef.Define(name, Transport.File("./test/<name>"))` — the tutorial page omits connectors, but the CLI is the real consumer).

Decisions confirmed with the user:
- **Keep file connectors** (transport-only `ConnectorRef.Define` + `Transport.File`); cut all other transports and the unresolved-connector machinery. No intropy-cli changes needed.
- **Keep TransactionalIntegration** as a block kind, but with `From`/`To` only — the API surface (`ApiRef`, `Provides`/`Consumes`, ITP501) is still cut.
- **Replace examples** with a tutorial-shaped order-flow system.
- **Branching:** preserve everything on a `full-topology` branch; land the minimal version on `main`.

Expected outcome: src shrinks from ~3,200 to roughly 1,600–1,800 LOC, `Intropy.Topology` and `.Generation` stay dependency-free, `.Aspire` drops the Microcks dependency.

## Repo & branching

All work in `/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/Intropy.Topology`.

5	/// <summary>Runs every topology rule and collects the diagnostics.</summary>
6	internal static class TopologyRules
7	{
8	    // Retired codes — do not reuse. Enforced at compile time by the block builders:
9	    // ITP204 (trigger kind not allowed for the block kind), ITP205 (connector direction
10	    // not allowed for the block kind). No longer meaningful since triggers were replaced
11	    // by edges (subscriptions/APIs) and activation/workload shape moved to the component
12	    // scaffold: ITP201 (invalid cron), ITP202 (missing trigger), ITP203 (multiple
13	    // TriggeredBy calls).
14	    private static readonly ITopologyRule[] Rules =
15	    [
16	        new Rules.DuplicateComponentNameRule(),
17	        new Rules.EmptySystemRule(),
18	        new Rules.DuplicatePortRule(),
19	        new Rules.DuplicateSubscriptionRule(),
20	        new Rules.TopicContractConflictRule(),
21	        new Rules.ConnectorConflictRule(),
22	        new Rules.ConnectorInputCapabilityRule(),
23	        new Rules.ConnectorOutputCapabilityRule(),
24	        new Rules.UnresolvedConnectorRule(),
25	        new Rules.MissingRequiredOutputRule(),
26	        new Rules.MissingRequiredSubscriptionRule(),
27	        new Rules.UnconsumedTopicRule(),
28	        new Rules.UnproducedTopicRule(),
29	        new Rules.ApiProviderRule(),
30	        new Rules.NoEdgesRule(),
31	        new Rules.PubSubConnectorNameCollisionRule(),
32	    ];
33	
34	    public static IReadOnlyList<TopologyDiagnostic> Run(SystemBuilder builder, SystemTopology topology)
35	    {
36	        var context = new ValidationContext(builder, topology);
37	        return Rules.SelectMany(rule => rule.Evaluate(context)).ToArray();
38	    }
39	}

// One entry point, two backends of the same discovered truth. F5 (no args, or `run`) translates
// the topology into Aspire resources and hands them to DCP; the other verbs generate/check/graph
// from the identical model without touching Aspire.
//
//   dotnet run                       -> Aspire (dashboard: components + Redis + mock sidecars)
//   dotnet run -- check              -> validate the topology
//   dotnet run -- graph              -> print the SystemTopology JSON
//   dotnet run -- generate ./out     -> write Dapr YAML + per-component config

var assembly = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly();

return args is ["run", ..] or []
    ? await IntropyAspire.RunAsync(assembly, args)
    : await IntropyGenerate.RunAsync(assembly, args);

26	dotnet run --project examples/OrderFulfillment.SystemHost -- generate ./out

28	
29	## Architecture Overview
30	
31	This is a typed, fluent DSL for declaring Intropy integration-system topologies in .NET 10. A SystemHost project declares a system's components and the edges between them in code; `Build()` validates the declaration and produces an immutable, serializable `SystemTopology` that downstream Kubernetes/Dapr generation tooling consumes. The library has zero external runtime dependencies.
32	
33	**The topology is only the edges *between* components** — subscriptions, publishes, APIs, connectors, service uses. What activates a component at runtime (cron schedule vs. long-running app) and its workload shape are *not* modeled here; they live in the component's own scaffold. There is no trigger concept and no `WorkloadType`.
34	
35	### Packages
36	
37	| Package | Purpose |
38	|---------|---------|
39	| **Intropy.Topology** | Staged builders, refs, the immutable topology model, validation, and `ISystemDefinition` discovery (dependency-free) |
40	| **Intropy.Topology.Generation** | `SystemTopology` → Dapr component YAML + per-component runtime config; the `check`/`graph`/`generate` verbs and the `IDevProfile` dev seam (dependency-free) |
41	| **Intropy.Topology.Aspire** | The F5 run backend: translates the discovered topology into Aspire resources (per-integration component overlay under `obj/dapr-components/`, subscriber-first startup ordering); the only package with an Aspire dependency |
42	
43	The user-facing name for the host project is **SystemHost** (`OrderFulfillment.SystemHost`): an ordinary console project holding the system declaration, whose `Program.cs` routes to the Aspire or generate backend. "Aspire AppHost" is plumbing — the `Aspire.AppHost.Sdk` csproj line exists so the run backend can fetch the orchestrator and dashboard (ADR 0005, amended).
44	
45	### Key Concepts
46	
47	**Per-block builders = compile-time legality**: each `Add*` on `SystemBuilder` returns that block's builder (`ExtractorBuilder`, `AggregatorBuilder`, ...), whose members are exactly the edges legal for that block — an extractor has `From`/`Provides`/`Publishes`, an aggregator has `Subscribes`/`Publishes`, a loader has `Subscribes`/`To`. Declaring an edge a block cannot have is a compile error, not a validation diagnostic. Retired diagnostic codes — never reuse: ITP201 (invalid cron), ITP202 (missing trigger), ITP203 (multiple `TriggeredBy`) died with the trigger concept; ITP204/ITP205 (illegal trigger kind / connector direction) remain compile-time.
48	
49	**Edges, not triggers**: async interfaces are topics (`Publishes`/`Subscribes`), sync interfaces are APIs (`Provides`/`Consumes`); both are contracts *between* the system's own components. Connectors (`From`/`To`) are the edges *out* to external systems. An API has exactly one provider (ITP501) and any number of consumers. Every topic must have both sides — a published topic with no subscriber is ITP208, a subscription nothing publishes is ITP209 (both errors). A loader needs no `To`: its destination may stay a private local component (decision 0008). The block kinds are Extractor, Aggregator, Loader, and TransactionalIntegration (this is a lean PoC — Reconciler, ContainerService, and platform-service `Uses` were deliberately cut and will be re-added when needed).
50	
51	**Component = the shared substance behind every block** (mirrors `Pipeline` in intropy-framework): `public abstract Component` (root namespace) is the recording state every builder writes into, and each block kind is a sealed subclass (`ExtractorComponent`, `AggregatorComponent`, `LoaderComponent`, `TransactionalIntegrationComponent`) exposed via the builder's `.Component` property as an optional typed handle (public surface: `Name`, `Kind`; recorded calls stay internal). The hierarchy lives in `Components.cs`; all builders live in `Building/ComponentBuilders.cs` (grouped files — related types share a file rather than one type per file). See `docs/decisions/0003-per-block-components.md` (layout section amended 2026-07-19).
52	
53	**Refs declared as static fields**: `TopicRef<T>.Define(pubsub, topic)`, `ApiRef<T>.Define(name)`, and `ConnectorRef.Define(name, externalSystem, transport)` live in scaffolded `Topics.cs` / `Apis.cs` / `Connectors.cs` files in the SystemHost. Resources (topics, APIs, connectors) materialize from usage — there is no `AddTopic`.
54	
55	**Declare → materialize → validate**: `TopologyMaterializer` (in `src/Intropy.Topology/Building/`) never fails (first-seen wins, deterministic ordering: declaration order for components, `StringComparer.Ordinal` sorting for resources). `TopologyRules` (in `src/Intropy.Topology/Validation/`) then collects every diagnostic; `Build()` throws `TopologyValidationException` carrying all of them when any is error-severity. `TryBuild`/`Validate` are the non-throwing variants.
56	
57	**Namespaces**: the flat `Intropy.Topology` namespace is the user-facing DSL surface (project root, including `Component` and the per-block components); `Intropy.Topology.Building` holds the fluent machinery users never name; `Intropy.Topology.Model` is the output model; `Intropy.Topology.Validation(.Rules)` is internal.
58	
59	**File layout is grouped, not one-type-per-file**: cohesive types share a file (`Components.cs`, `Refs.cs`, `Building/ComponentBuilders.cs`, `Model/Edges.cs`, `Model/Resources.cs`, `Model/Enums.cs`). When adding a type, put it in the existing file it belongs with; only give it its own file when no grouping fits.
60	
61	**Names are DNS-1123**: component/topic/connector/port names are validated eagerly at the call site by `NameRules` (`ArgumentException`); only semantic topology validation is deferred to `Build()`.
62	
63	### Testing
64	
65	Tests use xUnit with plain `Assert` (no mocking or assertion libraries). Test method naming follows `Method_WithCondition_ShouldExpectation`, with explicit `// Arrange / // Act / // Assert` comments. Test files mirror the source structure under `test/Intropy.Topology.Test/`; internals are reachable via `InternalsVisibleTo`. `EndToEndTests` is the living spec and includes a **byte-exact JSON snapshot** of the materialized model — deliberate model changes require updating the inline snapshot.

A loader needs no `To`: its destination may stay a private local component (decision 0008). The block kinds are Extractor, Aggregator, Loader, and TransactionalIntegration (this is a lean PoC — Reconciler, ContainerService, and platform-service `Uses` were deliberately cut and will be re-added when needed).

**Component = the shared substance behind every block** (mirrors `Pipeline` in intropy-framework): `public abstract Component` (root namespace) is the recording state every builder writes into, and each block kind is a sealed subclass (`ExtractorComponent`, `AggregatorComponent`, `LoaderComponent`, `TransactionalIntegrationComponent`) exposed via the builder's `.Component` property as an optional typed handle (public surface: `Name`, `Kind`; recorded calls stay internal). The hierarchy lives in `Components.cs`; all builders live in `Building/ComponentBuilders.cs` (grouped files — related types share a file rather than one type per file). See `docs/decisions/0003-per-block-components.md` (layout section amended 2026-07-19).

**Refs declared as static fields**: `TopicRef<T>.Define(pubsub, topic)`, `ApiRef<T>.Define(name)`, and `ConnectorRef.Define(name, externalSystem, transport)` live in scaffolded `Topics.cs` / `Apis.cs` / `Connectors.cs` files in the SystemHost. Resources (topics, APIs, connectors) materialize from usage — there is no `AddTopic`.

**Declare → materialize → validate**: `TopologyMaterializer` (in `src/Intropy.Topology/Building/`) never fails (first-seen wins, deterministic ordering: declaration order for components, `StringComparer.Ordinal` sorting for resources). `TopologyRules` (in `src/Intropy.Topology/Validation/`) then collects every diagnostic; `Build()` throws `TopologyValidationException` carrying all of them when any is error-severity. `TryBuild`/`Validate` are the non-throwing variants.

**Namespaces**: the flat `Intropy.Topology` namespace is the user-facing DSL surface (project root, including `Component` and the per-block components); `Intropy.Topology.Building` holds the fluent machinery users never name; `Intropy.Topology.Model` is the output model; `Intropy.Topology.Validation(.Rules)` is internal.

**File layout is grouped, not one-type-per-file**: cohesive types share a file (`Components.cs`, `Refs.cs`, `Building/ComponentBuilders.cs`, `Model/Edges.cs`, `Model/Resources.cs`, `Model/Enums.cs`). When adding a type, put it in the existing file it belongs with; only give it its own file when no grouping fits.

**Names are DNS-1123**: component/topic/connector/port names are validated eagerly at the call site by `NameRules` (`ArgumentException`); only semantic topology validation is deferred to `Build()`.

### Testing

Tests use xUnit with plain `Assert` (no mocking or assertion libraries). Test method naming follows `Method_WithCondition_ShouldExpectation`, with explicit `// Arrange / // Act / // Assert` comments. Test files mirror the source structure under `test/Intropy.Topology.Test/`; internals are reachable via `InternalsVisibleTo`. `EndToEndTests` is the living spec and includes a **byte-exact JSON snapshot** of the materialized model — deliberate model changes require updating the inline snapshot.

Topics, APIs, and connectors are declared as static fields; the backing resources materialize from
usage (there is no `AddTopic`). The Dapr binding component name is derived from the connector's name
(`binding.webshop`), never declared:

```csharp
public static class OrderFlow
{
    public static readonly TopicRef<RawOrder> Raw =
        TopicRef<RawOrder>.Define("order-fulfillment-pubsub", "order-raw");
    public static readonly TopicRef<FulfillmentOrder> Fulfillment =
        TopicRef<FulfillmentOrder>.Define("order-fulfillment-pubsub", "order-fulfillment");
}

public static class Connectors
{
    public static readonly ConnectorRef Webshop =
        ConnectorRef.Define("webshop", new ExternalSystem("webshop"), Transport.Sftp());  // → binding.webshop
    public static readonly ConnectorRef Erp =
        ConnectorRef.Define("erp", new ExternalSystem("erp"), Transport.Http());           // → binding.erp
}
```

All connectivity runs through Dapr — a transport selects the Dapr binding component's `spec.type`.
Built-in transports are `Transport.Http()`, `Transport.Sftp()`, and `Transport.Blob()`;
`Transport.Custom("bindings.kafka")` covers any other Dapr binding type. Transports declare direction
capabilities, validated at `Build()`: Dapr's HTTP binding is output-only, so an HTTP connector can be
written to (`To`) but not read from (`From`).

Only a connector's **name** is intrinsic to a component — it is the local port it reads from or writes
to. *What* it connects to (the external system) and *how* (the transport) are resolved together at
system assembly (`intropy system create`), not at block scaffolding. So a scaffolded block emits
`ConnectorRef.Define("erp")` (name only); assembly rewrites it to the fully resolved form above. A
connector that is still missing its external system or transport builds and validates but surfaces as
a warning (ITP107) until resolved.

## One model, two backends

The SystemHost has a single entry point; the same discovered, validated topology feeds either backend:

```csharp
var assembly = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly();
return args is ["run", ..] or []
    ? await IntropyAspire.RunAsync(assembly, args)   // → .NET Aspire + DCP (local F5)
    : await IntropyGenerate.RunAsync(assembly, args); // → generate | check | graph
```

```bash

dotnet run --project examples/OrderFulfillment.SystemHost -- check            # validate the topology
dotnet run --project examples/OrderFulfillment.SystemHost -- graph            # print the SystemTopology JSON
dotnet run --project examples/OrderFulfillment.SystemHost -- generate ./out   # write Dapr YAML + per-component config
```

The Aspire backend is a one-way **translator**: it discovers the model, generates dev Dapr
components in-memory, and speaks Aspire's language (`AddProject`, `AddContainer`, `AddMicrocks`,
`WithDaprSidecar`) to build the resource graph DCP runs — Redis behind pub/sub, containers for
declared external-system mocks, and one [Microcks](https://microcks.io) instance serving
contract-backed mocks for HTTP connectors and dev-mocked internal APIs. Aspire never sees the model — the same
one-way relationship Generation has with Dapr YAML, targeting a live object model instead of files.
So F5 and `kubectl apply` become two backends of the same generated truth.

A complete, runnable example lives in [`examples/OrderFulfillment.SystemHost`](examples/OrderFulfillment.SystemHost/).
It maps each component to a sibling worker project by folder convention (`order-extractor` →
`../order-extractor/`).

The block-specific builders expose only each block's legal edges, so these are compile errors — the
method simply does not exist:

```csharp
builder.AddLoader("l").Subscribes(t).Publishes(t);   // loaders publish nothing
builder.AddExtractor("e").Subscribes(t);             // extractors read connectors, not topics
builder.AddAggregator("a").From(connector);          // aggregators have no connectors
```

Per block: extractors read a connector (`From`) and publish; aggregators subscribe to one or more
topics and publish; loaders subscribe to one topic and may write through a connector (a private

read/write connectors. Any component may consume an API. Every topic must have both sides:

(ITP208/ITP209).

touch — is usually buried across Kubernetes manifests and Dapr YAML, where nothing checks it.
Intropy.Topology moves that declaration into typed code: each `Add*` call returns a block-specific
builder that exposes only the edges legal for that block. *Illegal topology is a compile error, not
a validation diagnostic*; only what types cannot check (completeness and cross-component conflicts)
is validated at `Build()`.

The topology records only the edges **between** components — subscriptions, publishes, and
connectors out to the outside world. How a component is activated at runtime and its workload shape

{

    public void Define(SystemBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor")
            .From(Connectors.OrderExtractorSource)
            .Publishes(Topics.Orders);

        builder.AddLoader("order-loader")
            .Subscribes(Topics.Orders)
            .To(Connectors.OrderLoaderDestination);
    }
}

        ConnectorRef.Define("order-loader-destination", Transport.File("./test/order-loader-destination"));

> use. The full model (aggregators, APIs, named publish ports, sftp/blob/http/custom transports,
> dev mocking) is preserved on the `full-topology` branch.

## Why?

The shape of an integration system — which components exist, which topics and external systems they
touch — is usually buried across Kubernetes manifests and Dapr YAML, where nothing checks it.
Intropy.Topology moves that declaration into typed code: each `Add*` call returns a block-specific
builder that exposes only the edges legal for that block. *Illegal topology is a compile error, not
a validation diagnostic*; only what types cannot check (completeness and cross-component conflicts)
is validated at `Build()`.

The topology records only the edges **between** components — subscriptions, publishes, and
connectors out to the outside world. How a component is activated at runtime and its workload shape
are not modeled here; they live in the component's own scaffold.

## Packages

| Package | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| [Intropy.Topology](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Intropy.Topology) | Staged builders, refs, discovery, the immutable topology model, and validation |
| Intropy.Topology.Generation | `SystemTopology` → Dapr component YAML + per-component runtime config; the `check`/`graph`/`generate` verbs |
| Intropy.Topology.Aspire | Translates a discovered topology into a live .NET Aspire application (Redis-backed pub/sub, Dapr sidecars) |

## Quick start

Declare the system as an `ISystemDefinition`:

```csharp
public sealed class OrderFlowSystem : ISystemDefinition
{
    public string SystemName => "order-flow";

    public void Define(SystemBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor")
            .From(Connectors.OrderExtractorSource)
            .Publishes(Topics.Orders);

        builder.AddLoader("order-loader")
            .Subscribes(Topics.Orders)
            .To(Connectors.OrderLoaderDestination);
    }
}
```

Topics and connectors are declared as static fields; the backing resources materialize from usage
(there is no `AddTopic`). The Dapr binding component name is derived from the connector's name
(`binding.order-extractor-source`), never declared:

```csharp
public static class Topics
{
    public static readonly TopicRef<Order> Orders = TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "orders");
}

public static class Connectors
{
    public static readonly ConnectorRef OrderExtractorSource =
        ConnectorRef.Define("order-extractor-source", Transport.File("./test/order-extractor-source"));
    public static readonly ConnectorRef OrderLoaderDestination =
        ConnectorRef.Define("order-loader-destination", Transport.File("./test/order-loader-destination"));
}
```

All connectivity runs through Dapr — a transport selects the Dapr binding component's `spec.type`.
The minimal model ships one transport: `Transport.File(rootPath)` (`bindings.localstorage`), the
default resolution `intropy sys create` applies. The folder is the endpoint, so a file connector
needs no external-system concept — the system runs with zero external configuration.

## One model, two backends

The SystemHost has a single entry point; the same discovered, validated topology feeds either backend:

```csharp
var assembly = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly();
return args is ["run", ..] or []
    ? await IntropyAspire.RunAsync(assembly, args)   // → .NET Aspire + DCP (local F5)
    : await IntropyGenerate.RunAsync(assembly, args); // → generate | check | graph
```

```bash
dotnet run --project examples/OrderFlow.SystemHost                     # Aspire dashboard (needs Docker + `dapr init`)
dotnet run --project examples/OrderFlow.SystemHost -- check            # validate the topology
dotnet run --project examples/OrderFlow.SystemHost -- graph            # print the SystemTopology JSON
dotnet run --project examples/OrderFlow.SystemHost -- generate ./out   # write Dapr YAML + per-component config
```

The Aspire backend is a one-way **translator**: it discovers the model, generates the system's Dapr
components, and speaks Aspire's language (`AddProject`, `AddContainer`, `WithDaprSidecar`) to build
the resource graph DCP runs — Redis behind pub/sub, one project with a Dapr sidecar per component,
subscribers started before their publishers. Each sidecar loads a staged overlay: the integration's
own `local/dapr-components/` plus the generated system components, where a generated component with
the same `metadata.name` replaces the local one. Aspire never sees the model — the same one-way
relationship Generation has with Dapr YAML, targeting a live object model instead of files. So F5
and `kubectl apply` become two backends of the same generated truth.

A complete, runnable example lives in [`examples/OrderFlow.SystemHost`](examples/OrderFlow.SystemHost/).
It maps each component to a sibling worker project by folder convention (`order-extractor` →
`../order-extractor/`), and its declaration files mirror `intropy sys create` output verbatim.

## Illegal topology does not compile

The block-specific builders expose only each block's legal edges, so these are compile errors — the
method simply does not exist:

```csharp
builder.AddLoader("l").Subscribes(t).Publishes(t);   // loaders publish nothing
builder.AddExtractor("e").Subscribes(t);             // extractors read connectors, not topics
```

Per block: extractors read a connector (`From`) and publish one topic; loaders subscribe to one
topic and may write through a connector (a private local destination needs no declared edge);
transactional integrations read/write connectors. Every topic must have both sides: `Build()`
rejects a published topic nobody subscribes to and a subscription nothing publishes
(ITP208/ITP209).

- .NET 10 or later
- For the Aspire `run` backend: Docker and the Dapr CLI (`dapr init`)

## Documentation

Full documentation lives in [`docs/`](docs/index.md):

- [Getting Started](docs/getting-started.md) — declare a complete order-flow topology
- [Components](docs/concepts/components.md) — component kinds and block builders
- [Topics](docs/concepts/topics.md) and [Connectors](docs/concepts/connectors.md) — refs, transports, materialize-from-usage
- [Validation](docs/concepts/validation.md) — the ITP diagnostic codes and Build/TryBuild/Validate
- [Materialization](docs/concepts/materialization.md) — the immutable, deterministic output model
- [ADR 0005](docs/decisions/0005-aspire-run-backend.md) — the discover → generate → run architecture

## Build and test

```bash
dotnet build Intropy.Topology.slnx
dotnet test Intropy.Topology.slnx
```

[MIT](LICENSE) © Integrio

A system is a class implementing `ISystemDefinition`: it declares components (extractors,
aggregators, loaders, transactional integrations) and the edges between them (topics, APIs,

## Why?

The shape of an integration system — which components exist, which topics and external systems they

Intropy.Topology moves that declaration into typed code: each `Add*` call returns a block-specific
builder that exposes only the edges legal for that block. *Illegal topology is a compile error, not
a validation diagnostic*; only what types cannot check (completeness and cross-component conflicts)
is validated at `Build()`.

The topology records only the edges **between** components — subscriptions, publishes, APIs, and
connectors out to external systems. How a component is activated at runtime and its workload shape
are not modeled here; they live in the component's own scaffold.

## Packages

| Package | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| [Intropy.Topology](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Intropy.Topology) | Staged builders, refs, discovery, the immutable topology model, and validation |
| Intropy.Topology.Generation | `SystemTopology` → Dapr component YAML + per-component runtime config; the `check`/`graph`/`generate` verbs |
| Intropy.Topology.Aspire | Translates a discovered topology into a live .NET Aspire application (Redis-backed pub/sub, mock containers, Dapr sidecars) |

## Quick start

Declare the system as an `ISystemDefinition`:

```csharp
public sealed class OrderFulfillmentSystem : ISystemDefinition
{
    public string SystemName => "order-fulfillment";

    public void Define(SystemBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor")
            .From(Connectors.Webshop)
            .Publishes(OrderFlow.Raw);

        builder.AddAggregator("order-aggregator")
            .Subscribes(OrderFlow.Raw, StockFlow.Raw)
            .Publishes("fulfillment", OrderFlow.Fulfillment)
            .Consumes(Apis.Freight);

        builder.AddLoader("erp-order-loader")
            .Subscribes(OrderFlow.Fulfillment)
            .To(Connectors.Erp);

        builder.AddTransactionalIntegration("freight-booking")
            .Provides(Apis.Freight)
            .To(Connectors.Freight);
    }
}
```

Topics, APIs, and connectors are declared as static fields; the backing resources materialize from
usage (there is no `AddTopic`). The Dapr binding component name is derived from the connector's name
(`binding.webshop`), never declared:

```csharp
public static class OrderFlow
{
    public static readonly TopicRef<RawOrder> Raw =
        TopicRef<RawOrder>.Define("order-fulfillment-pubsub", "order-raw");

        TopicRef<FulfillmentOrder>.Define("order-fulfillment-pubsub", "order-fulfillment");
}

public static class Connectors
{
    public static readonly ConnectorRef Webshop =
        ConnectorRef.Define("webshop", new ExternalSystem("webshop"), Transport.Sftp());  // → binding.webshop
    public static readonly ConnectorRef Erp =
        ConnectorRef.Define("erp", new ExternalSystem("erp"), Transport.Http());           // → binding.erp
}
```

All connectivity runs through Dapr — a transport selects the Dapr binding component's `spec.type`.
Built-in transports are `Transport.Http()`, `Transport.Sftp()`, and `Transport.Blob()`;

capabilities, validated at `Build()`: Dapr's HTTP binding is output-only, so an HTTP connector can be
written to (`To`) but not read from (`From`).

method simply does not exist:

```csharp
builder.AddLoader("l").Subscribes(t).Publishes(t);   // loaders publish nothing
builder.AddExtractor("e").Subscribes(t);             // extractors read connectors, not topics
builder.AddAggregator("a").From(connector);          // aggregators have no connectors
```

Per block: extractors read a connector (`From`) and publish; aggregators subscribe to one or more
topics and publish; loaders subscribe to one topic and may write through a connector (a private
local destination needs no declared edge); transactional integrations provide an API and
read/write connectors. Any component may consume an API. Every topic must have both sides:
`Build()` rejects a published topic nobody subscribes to and a subscription nothing publishes
(ITP208/ITP209).

## Requirements

- .NET 10 or later
- For the Aspire `run` backend: Docker and the Dapr CLI (`dapr init`)

## Documentation

Full documentation lives in [`docs/`](docs/index.md):

- [Getting Started](docs/getting-started.md) — declare a complete order-fulfillment topology
- [Components](docs/concepts/components.md) — component kinds and block builders
- [Topics](docs/concepts/topics.md) and [Connectors](docs/concepts/connectors.md) — refs, transports, materialize-from-usage
- [Validation](docs/concepts/validation.md) — the ITP diagnostic codes and Build/TryBuild/Validate
- [Materialization](docs/concepts/materialization.md) — the immutable, deterministic output model
- [ADR 0005](docs/decisions/0005-aspire-run-backend.md) — the discover → generate → run architecture

## Build and test

```bash
dotnet build Intropy.Topology.slnx
dotnet test Intropy.Topology.slnx
```
